\chapter{Which One, That One}
\label{ch:sa-which-one-that-one}
\hlchaptermodality{53}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can open a clause with a \sk{य}- word and answer it with the matching \sk{त}- word, so that two Sanskrit clauses hold together as one sentence.}

Complete SA-R53-correlative and say both correlative sentences, naming for each the axis it joins on.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[yaḥ]{\sk{यः} (yaḥ) — who, which}

\label{lesson:SA-C53-yah}



\begin{quote}
Say the deixis system out loud: the \textbf{a-} word for near, the \textbf{t-} word for far, the \textbf{k-} word that asks. Then say \textquotedblleft{}neither food nor water\textquotedblright{}.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \sk{यः}}
\textbf{\sk{यः}} (\emph{yaḥ}) — \textquotedblleft{}who, which\textquotedblright{}.

The deixis lesson taught you that Sanskrit points with three initial letters. \textbf{\sk{अ}-} points near, \textbf{\sk{त}-} points far, \textbf{\sk{क}-} asks. The system was presented as three legs, and it has always had four.

\textbf{\sk{य}-} is the fourth. It does not point and it does not ask. It \textbf{hands the question forward} — it opens a clause and says: hold on, I am about to tell you which one I mean.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\sk{कः}} — \emph{who?} — I am asking you
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\sk{यः}} — \emph{who / the one who} — I am about to tell you
\end{quote}

Nothing else about the word is new. Its \textbf{-\sk{ः}} ending is the masculine ending you have read on \textbf{\sk{नरः}}, \textbf{\sk{बालः}} and \textbf{\sk{मार्गः}} since the place words, and it agrees exactly as those do.

Say the four together, because from here on they behave as one family: \textbf{\sk{अ}- · \sk{त}- · \sk{क}- · \sk{य}-}.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
The missing fourth leg of a system you already half knew.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{kaḥ}, then \emph{yaḥ}, and say which one asks
  \item \emph{Say it:} the four openings — \emph{a-}, \emph{ta-}, \emph{ka-}, \emph{ya-}
  \item \emph{Read it:} \textbf{\sk{यः}}, and name the ending it shares with \textbf{\sk{नरः}}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \textbf{\sk{यः}} do that \textbf{\sk{कः}} does not? (It hands the question forward instead of asking it.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[saḥ]{\sk{सः} (saḥ) — he, that one}

\label{lesson:SA-C53-sah}



\begin{quote}
What does \textbf{\sk{यः}} do? And what does \textbf{\sk{तत्}} point at?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \sk{सः}}
\textbf{\sk{सः}} (\emph{saḥ}) — \textquotedblleft{}he, that one\textquotedblright{}.

You have known \textbf{\sk{तत्}} since the deixis lesson — the \textbf{t-} word that points at something over there. \textbf{\sk{सः}} is the same pointing word for a \textbf{masculine} person or thing: \emph{that man, he, that one}.

The odd part is the \textbf{\sk{स}-}. Everywhere else in this family the far-pointer is \textbf{\sk{त}-}: \textbf{\sk{तत्}}, \textbf{\sk{तत्र}}, and every other form of the word. Only the masculine and feminine nominative singulars break out and begin with \textbf{\sk{स}-} — \textbf{\sk{सः}} and \textbf{\sk{सा}}. It is one of the oldest irregularities in the language, and it is inherited rather than invented: Greek's article does exactly the same thing, with \emph{ho} and \emph{hē} beside a \emph{t-} everywhere else.

So the rule to hold is small and strange: \textbf{the word is a t- word that starts with \sk{स}- only when it is the subject.}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
The pointer that will answer \textbf{\sk{यः}} in the next lesson.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{saḥ}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{yaḥ}, then \emph{saḥ}, and say which one opens and which one answers
  \item \emph{Read it:} \textbf{\sk{तत्}} and \textbf{\sk{सः}}, and say what the two have in common
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \textbf{\sk{सः}} mean, and which letter does it begin with only as a subject? (\textquotedblleft{}He, that one\textquotedblright{}, and \textbf{\sk{स}-}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[yaḥ … saḥ]{\sk{यः} … \sk{सः} (yaḥ … saḥ) — the correlative}

\label{lesson:SA-C53-yah-sah}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{\sk{यः}}, then \textbf{\sk{सः}}. Which one opens, and which one answers?
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: two clauses, one hinge}]
Put the two words in one sentence, each opening its own clause, and you have Sanskrit's entire relative-clause system.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\sk{यः} \sk{गच्छति} \sk{सः} \sk{पश्यति}}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{yaḥ gacchati saḥ paśyati}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{the one who goes, sees}
\end{quote}

Read it literally and it is stranger and simpler than the English: \emph{which one goes, that one sees.} The \textbf{\sk{य}-} clause raises a candidate; the \textbf{\sk{त}-} clause picks it up and says what happens to it.

\textbf{This is not the English shape with the words translated.} English hangs the relative clause off a noun — \emph{the man who goes} — and the clause sits inside the main sentence. Sanskrit sets two whole clauses side by side and pins them together with the \textbf{\sk{य}-}/\textbf{\sk{त}-} pair. There is no noun for the clause to hang from and none is needed.

Three consequences, all of which you can check on the sentence above:

\begin{enumerate}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{The \sk{य}- clause usually comes first.} English almost always puts the main clause first; Sanskrit almost always puts the relative one first.
  \item \textbf{Both halves are complete sentences.} \emph{yaḥ gacchati} would stand on its own as \textquotedblleft{}he goes\textquotedblright{} if \textbf{\sk{यः}} were \textbf{\sk{सः}}.
  \item \textbf{Nothing is subordinated by word order.} The pair of pronouns does all the work, so the halves can be swapped for emphasis without the grammar breaking.
\end{enumerate}

From here, every \textquotedblleft{}the one that…\textquotedblright{}, \textquotedblleft{}whoever…\textquotedblright{}, and \textquotedblleft{}what I said\textquotedblright{} you will meet in Sanskrit is this same hinge with different endings on it.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
A sentence with two clauses in it, for the first time in this track.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{yaḥ gacchati saḥ paśyati}
  \item \emph{Say it:} it again, and name which half is the y- clause
  \item \emph{Read it:} \textbf{\sk{यः} \sk{गच्छति} \sk{सः} \sk{पश्यति}}, then say what it means in English
  \item \emph{Contrast:} English hangs the clause on a noun; Sanskrit pins two clauses with a pronoun pair
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which clause comes first in Sanskrit, the \textbf{\sk{य}-} one or the \textbf{\sk{त}-} one? (The \textbf{\sk{य}-} one.) Say the sentence once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[yatra … tatra]{\sk{यत्र} … \sk{तत्र} (yatra … tatra) — where … there}

\label{lesson:SA-C53-yatra-tatra}



\begin{quote}
Say the correlative sentence from the last lesson. Then say \textbf{\sk{अत्र}} and \textbf{\sk{तत्र}}, and what each one means.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the hinge is not about people}]
\textbf{\sk{यः} … \sk{सः}} joined two clauses through a \emph{person}. Change the pair and the same hinge joins them through a \emph{place}, with no other change at all.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\sk{यत्र} \sk{ग्रामः} \sk{तत्र} \sk{मार्गः}}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{yatra grāmaḥ tatra mārgaḥ}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{where there is a village, there is a road}
\end{quote}

\textbf{\sk{तत्र}} is not new — you have had it since the deixis lesson. \textbf{\sk{यत्र}} is \textbf{\sk{तत्र}} with the \textbf{\sk{य}-} opening swapped in, exactly as \textbf{\sk{यः}} was \textbf{\sk{सः}} with the same swap.

That is the real lesson of this chapter, and it is worth saying plainly: \textbf{the correlative is a slot, not a word.} Any \textbf{\sk{त}-} word you already know has a \textbf{\sk{य}-} partner, and putting the pair in two clauses joins them:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{\sk{य}- clause opens} & \textbf{\sk{त}- clause answers} & \textbf{joins by} \\
\midrule
\textbf{\sk{यः}} & \textbf{\sk{सः}} & person \\
\textbf{\sk{यत्र}} & \textbf{\sk{तत्र}} & place \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

You have met two of these. The pattern that generates them is one you can now recognise anywhere.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
The same two-clause hinge, on a second axis.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{yatra grāmaḥ tatra mārgaḥ}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \textbf{\sk{तत्र}}, then read \textbf{\sk{यत्र}} and say what the swap did
  \item \emph{Read it:} \textbf{\sk{यत्र} \sk{ग्रामः} \sk{तत्र} \sk{मार्गः}}, then say what it means
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How do you make a \textbf{\sk{य}-} word from a \textbf{\sk{त}-} word? (Swap the opening letter.) Say the village-and-road sentence once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ya- · ta-]{\sk{य}- · \sk{त}- — the correlative, reviewed}

\label{lesson:SA-R53-correlative}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{\sk{यः}} and \textbf{\sk{सः}}, and say which one opens its clause.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
The deixis lesson taught you three pointing letters and called it a system. It was three quarters of one. \textbf{\sk{य}-} is the fourth, and adding it turns a set of question-and-answer words into a way of building sentences with two clauses in them.

The whole of it fits in one line: \textbf{a \sk{य}- word raises a candidate, and the matching \sk{त}- word picks it up.}

Everything else in this chapter was that line applied twice — once through a person, once through a place — plus one small irregularity worth keeping: the far-pointer is a \textbf{\sk{त}-} word that wears \textbf{\sk{स}-} when it is the subject.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{yaḥ gacchati saḥ paśyati}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{yatra grāmaḥ tatra mārgaḥ}
  \item \emph{Recall:} name the four openings of the pointing system, in order
  \item \emph{Contrast:} \textbf{\sk{कः}} asks, \textbf{\sk{यः}} hands forward
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say both correlative sentences, and for each one name the axis it joins on — person or place.
\end{tcolorbox}
